title: About
text:
About Me



  The person behind the horse photo.





Who I Am


I'm Alnura, a 3rd year Data Science and Society student at Central European University, 
originally from Kazakhstan. I ended up in data science because it turns out numbers 
can be applied to pretty much everything — politics, behaviour, games, economies, 
people's feelings about democracy. That's the appeal. You pick a question that matters 
and data gives you a way to actually look at it.



When I'm not doing that, I'm cooking something that may or may not have followed 
the recipe, and thinking about horses.





What I Work With



  
  
    Languages
    Python, R, SQL
  

  
  
    Data & Analysis
    pandas, NumPy, EDA, regression modelling, survey data analysis
  

  
  
    Visualisation & BI
    Tableau, Plotly, Shiny, Matplotlib, Seaborn, Yandex DataLens
  

  
  
    Tools
    Excel, Google Sheets, PostgreSQL
  






Where I'm Headed


I'm interested in decision science — the intersection of data, behaviour, and 
how people and organisations actually make choices. The kind of work where the 
output isn't just a chart but something that changes what someone decides to do next.



Still figuring out the exact shape of it, but the direction is clear enough.

Do people judge democracy by GDP numbers or by how their wallet actually feels? Using World Values Survey data across 60+ countries, this study finds that subjective economic perception — not objective indicators like GDP or unemployment — is the only statistically significant predictor of satisfaction with democracy. The vibes, it turns out, win.



World Values Survey Wave 7 (2017-2022), World Bank, V-Dem Institute — 88,499 respondents across 60+ countries




Do people judge democracy based on GDP, or how they personally feel about the economy?
Does democracy quality actually predict satisfaction with democracy?
Which individual factors (age, education, income) matter for democratic satisfaction?





Economic perception is the only statistically significant predictor across all three models
GDP, unemployment, and democracy quality score show no significant effect once perception is controlled
Older and more educated people report higher satisfaction with democracy
The perception gap — not the numbers — is what drives democratic legitimacy
